What Is CAC Payback?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 16 July 2026 · 5-minute read · Revenue

CAC payback is the number of months it takes for the gross profit from a new customer to repay the cost of acquiring that customer. The common formula is customer acquisition cost divided by monthly revenue per customer multiplied by gross margin. A shorter payback means growth ties up less cash and survives more churn. The number is only useful if the cost side includes everything spent to win the customer.

What CAC payback means

Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the sales and marketing spend in a period divided by the number of new customers won. Payback converts that cost into time. Bessemer describes it as "the rate at which the costs spent to acquire a customer are repaid by that customer", and measures it against gross margin-adjusted revenue rather than top-line revenue.

Gross margin matters because a customer's revenue does not all come back to the business. Hosting, support, model inference and delivery staff take their share first. Two firms with the same price and the same CAC can have very different paybacks if one keeps 80% of each pound of revenue and the other keeps 50%.

An illustrative calculation for a mid-size software firm:

InputValue
Sales and marketing spend in the quarter£300,000
New customers won20
CAC£15,000
Monthly revenue per new customer£1,500
Gross margin75%
Monthly gross profit per customer£1,125
CAC payback15,000 ÷ 1,125 = 13.3 months

On Bessemer's targets, 13.3 months is acceptable for a mid-market seller and slow for an SMB one.

Why it matters for a commercial team

Acquisition is paid for up front and recovered slowly. Payback is the period during which cash is tied up in a customer who might still leave. A customer who churns in month 10 of a 13-month payback never repays their cost. ChartMogul describes under about 12 months as strong for SMB-focused SaaS and 12 to 24 months as typical for larger-contract enterprise software.

Payback is also the most useful way to compare channels. Blended CAC averages paid campaigns with referrals and inbound demand, which can hide a channel that loses money. Andreessen Horowitz notes that blended CAC "doesn't inform how well your paid campaigns are working and whether they're profitable", and that investors treat paid CAC as more important when judging viability.

For lowob, each decision to fund or cut a channel belongs in the commercial record: the payback assumed, the owner, and the payback observed two quarters later. Without that record, the same channel debate repeats every budget cycle with fresh numbers and no memory.

How to calculate it honestly

Most disagreement about CAC payback comes from a handful of choices. Making them explicit, and holding them constant, matters more than the exact convention chosen.

ChoiceFlattering versionHonest version
Costs includedMedia spend onlySales and marketing salaries, commissions, tools, agencies, events, and discounts or credits given to win the deal
Revenue basisTotal revenueGross margin-adjusted revenue
Customers countedAll new logos, including referralsPaid CAC by channel, alongside blended CAC
TimingSpend and customers in the same monthSpend lagged by your typical sales cycle
SegmentOne company-wide figureSeparate figures for SMB, mid-market and enterprise

Bessemer notes that CAC typically includes sales, marketing and sometimes customer success costs. If customer success time goes into onboarding new accounts, include that share. If it goes into renewals, leave it out and track it against retention instead.

Three common mistakes are worth checking for:

  1. Counting first-month revenue only. Ramped contracts and usage pricing start low. Use the expected run-rate after onboarding, and say so.
  2. Ignoring expansion and churn. Payback on a single customer's starting revenue misses later upsell and early loss. Read it alongside net revenue retention.
  3. Mixing services and software margin. If implementation fees carry a different margin from the subscription, calculate gross profit for each.

For a firm without subscription revenue, such as an advisory practice, the same logic works per client: the cost to win the engagement divided by monthly gross profit from it. If most clients do one project and leave, payback must happen inside that project.

lowob takeaways

  • Payback is time, not a ratio. It tells you how long cash is at risk in each new customer.
  • Margin belongs in the formula. Revenue that goes straight to delivery costs does not repay acquisition.
  • Compare by channel. Blended figures can hide a channel that never pays back.
  • Read it with retention. A customer who leaves before payback is a net loss, whatever the average says.

Common questions

How do you calculate CAC payback period?

Divide customer acquisition cost by the monthly gross profit from a new customer, which is monthly revenue multiplied by gross margin. The result is in months.

What is a good CAC payback period?

Bessemer's targets are under 12 months for SMB-focused companies, under 18 for mid-market and under 24 for enterprise. Shorter is safer when churn is high.

Should CAC payback use revenue or gross margin?

Gross margin. Revenue-based payback overstates how quickly a customer repays their cost, especially where delivery or inference costs are high.

What is the difference between CAC payback and LTV to CAC?

Payback measures how long recovery takes. LTV to CAC compares lifetime profit with acquisition cost. Bessemer suggests investing in acquisition when the lifetime value ratio is 3x or higher.

Sources and notes

  • ChartMogul, CAC Payback, undated. Vendor metrics library; source of the formula and ranges quoted.
  • Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million, 2021. Venture firm analysis of cloud companies; benchmarks reflect a high-growth sample.
  • Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics, August 2015, updated 2024. Investor guidance on CAC definitions.
